subject: Retirement age: 63 versus 65 with the retention bonus

turns.text: Morning, Kenji. I've updated the scenarios since our April 22 call to include the retention bonus. Can I walk you through them, and then ask what you and Mariko have worked out?
Please. I read your summary, but I'd like to hear it. Is the bonus counted at the full hundred and fifty thousand?

Pre-tax, yes, but only in the 63 scenario, paid in installments for as long as you stay. I haven't counted it at 60, because on the terms as I read them you'd forfeit it. I still haven't seen the retention agreement itself, so treat those terms as provisional.
I have the agreement. I'll upload it to the portal today.
Thank you. With the bonus, 63 funds the fifteen thousand a month target with a reasonable margin. 65 has a comfortable margin, as before. My suggestion is that 63 is the age to test, rather than 60.
That's fair. 60 is off the table in my head unless Northgate is sold and the role disappears. But I'm not ready to say 63 is the answer.
Understood. So what I'll hold today is this: 63 is under serious consideration, and the formal planning date is still 65.
Yes. Mariko and I talked on Sunday. She wants me out before 65, but she's nervous about the healthcare gap. She'd be happier with 63 than 65.
What worries her most about healthcare?
The two thousand eight hundred a month you estimated for private cover until Medicare. She wants to see that number in the plan, not just in my head.
It's in the 63 scenario for the full two years. I can show it as its own line so she can see it.
Please do. My brother also called. He thinks I'm crazy to stay on for a bonus at Northgate.
What do you think?
I think the bonus is real money and I'd be here until 63 anyway. I'm not letting him decide this.
Then here is what I'd suggest. You and Mariko take a few days. If you reach a decision, tell me on our May 1 call and I'll change the planning date then, not before.
Agreed. I'll tell you on Friday. Nothing changes in the file until I say so.
Grace, good to speak. I'll go in order of priority, and you can redirect me. On February 19 we covered Folake's tuition and cash flow; today the topic is survivor benefits from Social Security.
Oh... yes, that's fine. I'm not sure I've prepared as much as I should have.
We haven't talked about when to claim Social Security yet.
When should I claim Social Security? Everyone has a different opinion.

The honest answer is that it depends. Claiming earlier gives smaller checks for longer, and claiming later gives larger checks for a shorter period. The break-even is usually in the late seventies or early eighties, but that doesn't capture your health, your spouse's benefit or your other income.
So what do you look at?
Your life expectancy, how much you'd rely on the money, whether a spouse would inherit the larger benefit, and your taxes. I'd rather model it than guess.
Could I claim a survivor benefit now?

You may be eligible from age 60, but the amount is reduced if you claim early, and while you work before full retirement age the earnings limit could reduce it further. I'd want to check your exact numbers with the agency.
I'm working, so I'd rather wait.

That's reasonable. I'll note it as postponed, not decided forever. For the record, here is what we established. We agreed to hold off on claiming the Social Security survivor benefit while you are still working. I'll book us for Tuesday, March 3, if that suits you.
Yes... that's fair. I haven't made up my mind on that.

Hello Kenji. I have a short agenda today: comfort with portfolio risk. Is that still what you want to cover? Since March 4, when we focused on correcting the retirement-age record, the next topic is comfort with portfolio risk.

There's something that's been bothering me. March was ugly. At one point the portfolio was down well over two hundred thousand from the January high, and I realised it wasn't just a number. I'm wondering whether seventy-five percent in stocks is still right for me at 58.
I appreciate you saying that, because it's different from what you told me in January, when you said you'd sit tight through a twenty percent fall.
I know. Saying it and watching it are different. With the reorganisation on top, I'd feel better with smaller swings.

Then let's take that seriously. Two questions: how much less risk, and is this a temporary reaction or a lasting change? If we cut risk after a fall, we lock in the loss. If the change is lasting, the questionnaire should reflect it.
I think it's lasting. Maybe sixty percent? I don't want to be too conservative either.
Sixty is reasonable to look at, but I won't act on 'maybe'. I'll prepare a comparison of 60-40 and 70-30 portfolios, including the effect on your retirement scenarios, and we can decide next time.
Mariko wants to redo the garden now that the weather has turned.

Sounds nice. Just flag anything over a few thousand dollars so I can plan liquidity around it. Second item: suitability. Regarding a lower equity allocation, there's a step I have to take first: a suitability review. I compare what you're asking for with your goals, your capacity for loss and your liquidity needs.
And if it doesn't pass?
Then I tell you why, and we look at alternatives that do. It isn't a verdict on you. It's how I show that any advice I give was appropriate for your circumstances at the time.
Okay, that makes sense. Let's do it properly.

My notes from today read as follows. You're still weighing reducing equity exposure from about 75 percent to around 60, which I've recorded as an idea and not an instruction. From my side, I'll prepare a comparison of 60 and 70 percent equity portfolios against your retirement scenarios. I'll book us for Tuesday, March 31, if that suits you. I'll put a written summary in the portal today.
Right. The undecided items stay undecided until I say so.
Good morning, Grace. I've put the numbers for today on one page. Shall we begin? On May 8 we covered the gradual investing plan; today the topic is Tobi's graduation and beneficiaries.
Yes. I'll try to keep up.

On documentation: please get me your will and the beneficiary designations on your own accounts. I need it so I can update them now that Samuel is no longer your beneficiary, and I'd rather work from the paper than from memory.
I'll look for it. It might be in Samuel's study, and I haven't gone through all of that yet.
Scans work. Please use the secure upload link in your portal, and tell me if any page is missing so I can note it.
Work has asked if I'd stay on past 65 as a consultant. I told them I'd think about it.

That's a flattering offer. We can look at it when we revisit your retirement timing. Moving on. I'd like to check your spending against what we assumed in the plan. I'm seeing about $6,200 a month on average, set against your salary as a hospital administrator, which is now your only earned income. Is that how it feels?
Mostly. There are still bills coming in under Samuel's name, I think.
Understood. One quarter is not a trend; I'll track it against the plan.
Hm. Could you say that again, more slowly?

My notes from today read as follows. Nothing in your plan changes today; Tobi's graduation and beneficiaries was a check that nothing is drifting. From your side, you'll send over your will and the beneficiary designations on your own accounts. Let's pencil in Tuesday, May 19 for our next meeting. A written recap will be in the portal shortly; tell me if anything looks off.
Yes, I think that's right.

subject: Feeling ready to invest a little

turns.text: Good morning, Grace. I've put the numbers for today on one page. Shall we begin? Last time, on April 30, we focused on thinking about when to retire. Today's focus is feeling ready to invest a little.
I've been looking at the account, and it feels like the money is just sitting there. A part of me wants to put some of it to work. Not a lot.
That's a different feeling from January. What has changed?
I feel steadier. And I realise I can't live on fear forever.
I'm glad you can say that. How would you feel if part of the money went down for a while?
Uncomfortable. But I could live with a small amount. Maybe a quarter in stocks?
Let's study it properly rather than just doing it. I'll prepare a gradual plan, with the possible ups and downs.
I've been sleeping through the night more often than not.

That's good to hear. Next, suitability. Before I can recommend anything about raising your stock exposure, I have to complete a suitability assessment. That means documenting your objectives, your time horizon, how much loss you can absorb, and what you hold elsewhere.
Is that mostly paperwork?
It's partly paperwork, but it's also a check on me. If your answers don't support a recommendation, I shouldn't make it, even if you'd like me to.
That's fair. What do you need from me?

Honest answers. Where your comfort and your capacity differ, I record the more cautious of the two. For the record, here is what we established. You're still weighing raising stock exposure to about a quarter of the portfolio, which I've recorded as an idea and not an instruction. From my side, I'll prepare a gradual plan to raise stock exposure. Does Friday, May 8 work for the next one? I'll put a written summary in the portal today.
Yes... that's fair. I haven't made up my mind on that.
It's Priya. Hello, Grace. Before we start, is there anything that has changed in your circumstances since May 21? Today the topic is retirement age decision.
I've decided to work until 63. Not 62, not 65. It's a compromise. Another year helps the numbers, and I'd like to finish a project at the hospital.
Thank you. In April you were considering 62, and before that 65. I'll record 63 and your reason.
Yes. And if Tobi's business needs support, I may revisit.
Let me give you the headline numbers. The portfolio is about $1.47 million today, roughly flat since we last looked. The equity share is about 15 percent, in line with what we agreed.
Can you remind me why we hold the retirement account you rolled into your own name?
Good question. It's still invested conservatively, and it's the long-term money that the gradual move into stocks draws on.
So... what does that mean for me, in plain terms?

No action needed on your side. With the portfolio at $1.47 million, I'd only propose changes if the mix drifts well away from target, and I'd ask you first. Moving on. Let's glance at your cash flow. Over the past few months your spending has averaged around $6,200 a month, measured against your salary as a hospital administrator, which is now your only earned income. Does that feel right to you?
I think so, although I've been paying for the funeral costs in pieces.
That variance is explained, so I'll leave the plan unchanged and compare it with next quarter's figures.
Oh. I see, I think.
To summarise today in order: You've decided to work until 63, rather than 62 or 65, to strengthen the numbers and finish a hospital project. Let's pencil in Friday, June 5 for our next meeting.
That's what I understood, yes.

It's Priya. Hello Grace. I have a short agenda today: revisiting the mortgage. Is that still what you want to cover? Since April 8, when we focused on retitling the inherited account, the next topic is revisiting the mortgage.
Oh... yes, that's fine. I'm not sure I've prepared as much as I should have.
As we agreed, I'd like to revisit the mortgage. Here is the picture: the three point one percent rate, the amount of cash you'd use, and the effect on your emergency reserve.
I've been thinking about it. In February I wanted it gone. Now I think I'd rather keep the mortgage.
What changed?
Seeing the numbers helped. If I pay it off, I'd lose too much flexibility for Folake. And three point one percent isn't much.
Then I'll record that you've decided to keep the mortgage for now, with the reason.
Samuel's birthday was on April 11. I made his jollof rice and we told stories.

That sounds like a lovely way to remember him. A separate matter. On the portfolio: roughly $1.46 million, up about 0.4 percent since we last looked, and the asset mix is close to its target with equities near 15 percent.
Can you remind me why we hold the intermediate bond fund?
Good question. It pays more than cash and moves less than stocks, which suits where you are right now.
Is it all right? Is it, I mean, normal?

Nothing urgent. I'll keep monitoring it, and you'll hear from me with a recommendation before anything is executed. My notes from today read as follows. You've decided to keep the mortgage rather than pay it off, because the three point one percent rate is low and you want flexibility for Folake. Does Monday, April 27 work for the next one? I'll put a written summary in the portal today.
I believe so. You'll send it to me in writing?
I'll send the summary today. Goodbye, Grace.

subject: What to do with the secondary-sale proceeds

turns.text: It's Daniel. Morning, Lucas. Let's get into it. What's on your mind first? We last spoke on April 14, about decision on the secondary offer. For today I have what to do with the secondary-sale proceeds.
Okay. Can we spend less time on what to do with the secondary-sale proceeds and more on the money stuff?
Quick follow-up from our last meeting: were you able to sign and return the secondary sale paperwork before the deadline?
I signed it Monday, and the company confirmed receiving it.
Perfect. Done. Let me change gears. Before the proceeds: the April tax payment was due yesterday. How did you cover the shortfall?
Invoices came in, mostly. Twenty-two of the twenty-five thousand. I took the rest out of the cash account.

So the plan B was needed, but only a little. I'll record the shortfall as paid. Now, the secondary closed. Seventy-five thousand gross. What happens to it is what I want to settle. Founder shares have a very low basis, so most of it is taxable gain. Plan on about a quarter going to tax.
A quarter? So I clear fifty-six?
Roughly. After setting the tax aside, the reserve is at about eight months, and the target you set in March was nine.
Then the rest goes into Vantora. It's down. Lottery-ticket price.
I'd push back on that. This would put more of your liquid money in two things in the same sector, your company and that stock.
You sound like my accountant.
I'm being your advisor. You said in March the priority was the reserve.
Okay. Okay. Reserve first. And the leftover?
Index fund, not Vantora.
Fine. Fill the reserve to nine months, tax set-aside off the top, whatever's left goes in the index fund.

So, to be clear: You've decided to set aside about a quarter of the secondary-sale proceeds for tax, fill the cash reserve to nine months, and put anything left into the index fund and not into Vantora. The working plan I'm recording is the April tax shortfall paid, with about twenty-two thousand dollars from invoices and the rest from the cash account. Does Tuesday, April 21 work for the next one? I'll put a written summary in the portal today.
Sure, that's right.

Alright. Before our next meeting, please.
Fine. This week. Remind me if I forget.
On liquidity: you hold about $62,000 in cash and short-term holdings, which covers roughly 10 months of spending at the current level.
Is that enough, or are you just being careful?

For you, given your irregular income and the tax bills that nobody withholds for you, I'd aim for around 9 months, so you're at or above that. I don't see a reason to hold more cash than this, because it has a cost in lost growth.
Huh. Fair.
Let's check in on the markets. The month has brought choppy trading that still left markets modestly higher for the half-year. How is that sitting with you?
Everyone's panicking. I'm not, quite. Should I be?

It's understandable. My suggestion is not to act on a month of headlines. Your allocation was designed for periods like this, and a twenty percent equity decline would be about $213,000. What I do want to confirm is that your cash reserve is enough that you'd never have to sell into a weak market.
Yeah, okay. I'll live with it.

Quick recap: No decisions were needed today. We went through disability cover follow-up and everything is on track. From your side, you'll send over your current health and disability insurance policy summaries. Does Monday, June 22 work for the next one?
Yeah, accurate.
Good. Talk soon.
